title: DSFL: A Dual-Server Byzantine-Resilient Federated Learning Framework via Group-Based Secure Aggregation

C-a.quote: DSFL introduces three core innovations: (1) a dual-server secure aggregation protocol that preserves update confidentiality without encryption or pairwise key exchange, (2) a group-wise, credit-based filtering mechanism to identify and suppress Byzantine participants based on deviation scoring, and (3) a dynamic reward–penalty strategy to enforce fair, adaptive participation over training rounds.
C-a.locator: Sec. 1; AMENDMENT 3 LEAVES EXACTLY ONE DEFENSE-PURPOSED MECHANISM, so the count does not reach two. Innovation (2) is the counted one and its purpose is defense twice over, here and at Sec. 4, "1) Secure Byzantine Robustness: To counteract the influence of Byzantine participants on the global model, it is crucial to scrutinise the model parameters submitted by each participant and select the most reliable ones. This study proposes a k-nearest weight selection approach that effectively resists Byzantine participants". Innovation (1) is privacy-purposed on its own words ("preserves update confidentiality"), as is the DP noise; and innovation (3), the reward-penalty credit stage, is FAIRNESS-purposed here ("to enforce fair, adaptive participation over training rounds") and again in the design section's enumeration of what the aggregation rule ensures, "(iii) encourage participant engagement". The third listed component of Algorithm 2, secure model aggregation, is a plain average over the selected set ("TP computes w = 2k" over Pi in P). So the pipeline runs one detector, one fairness ledger, one average, over a privacy substrate

C-b.locator: Sec. 4; what the paper pairs is three PROPERTIES -- obliviousness, Byzantine mitigation and engagement -- enumerated as design goals, which is the DP-BREM pattern and not a reason selected from constituent properties. The framework-level motivation is the same shape, "how to simultaneously achieve privacy preservation, Byzantine robustness, and computational efficiency, particularly on edge devices with limited resources" (Sec. 1). Three targeted probes for a constituent-complementarity reason returned nothing usable: "complement" occurs twice and both are about secret shares or a figure, "alone|insufficient|not enough" occurs once and is about a single server's inability to invert the shares, and "repeatedly|over multiple rounds|historical" occurs ZERO times, so the credit ledger is never justified as covering an adversary that alternates across rounds -- which is the reason DP2Guard gives for the structurally similar stage. C-b = NO does not decide this row, since C-a = NO already excludes it

C-c.quote: While FedAvg degrades sharply with just 10% Byzantine clients—dropping to as low as 9.39% on CIFAR-100 non-IID, DSFL sustains robust accuracy even at 30% adversaries.
C-c.locator: Sec. 6; the assembled framework's own accuracy and attack success rate are the evidence, over MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 in IID and non-IID splits at 5/10/20/30% Byzantine participants, against FedAvg, SecAgg, Trimmed Mean, Median, FLOD, DPBFL, HE-based FL and LSFL ("TABLE III Test accuracy (%) under 20% Byzantine participants for various aggregation protocols across datasets (mean ± std)"), with an ASR-style series in "Fig. 3. Attacker success rate over training epochs across different aggregation protocols under label-flipping attacks"

C-d.quote: TABLE IV Test accuracy (%) of DSFL and FedAvg under varying Byzantine ratios on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 (IID / non-IID).
C-d.locator: Sec. 6; this is the only "varying" in the paper (1 occurrence) and what it varies is the ADVERSARY'S SHARE, an environment parameter, not an upstream stage of the defense. A caption enumeration of all sixteen numbered floats found only cross-system comparisons (DSFL against FedAvg, SecAgg, Trimmed Mean, Median, FLOD, DPBFL, HE-based FL and LSFL) and two overhead tables. The negative search was explicit: "ablation" 0 hits, "w/o" 0 hits, "disabl" 0 hits over 88175 characters. No arm removes, substitutes or re-parameterizes the k-nearest selection, the credit ledger or the grouping while holding the rest fixed

C-e.quote: This resilience can be attributed to the combined use of differential privacy noise, fair participant selection, and secure aggregation, which jointly obscure and filter malicious updates before they can affect the global model.
C-e.locator: Sec. 6; a mechanism-attribution claim naming three constituents and asserting what their combination does. A second one is at Sec. 4 on the counted stage, "This study proposes a k-nearest weight selection approach that effectively resists Byzantine participants", and a third at Sec. 6 on scaling, "This ability to scale robustly with adversarial pressure stands in contrast to most prior defences"

coder_note:
THIS ROW IS THE FIRST WHERE AMENDMENT 3 HAS TO CHOOSE BETWEEN A PAPER'S STATED PURPOSE FOR INCLUDING A COMPONENT AND ITS LATER ATTRIBUTION OF AN OBSERVED EFFECT TO THAT COMPONENT, AND IT DECIDED A NEAR-PRIMARY, SO THE REASONING IS RECORDED IN FULL. C-d = NO is established on a full negative search, and C-c and C-e are YES, so had C-a reached two this paper would have been the frame's FIFTH PRIMARY. The whole row turns on the reward-penalty credit stage. Structurally it is the DROP / DP2Guard / CLIP-Fed shape: a per-round detector followed by a cross-round ledger that can remove a participant permanently (Algorithm 2, lines 15-28: the credit is incremented for selected participants and decremented otherwise, and "if γi < 0 then P.remove(Pi)"). If it counted, C-a = YES and the composition is real.

It does not count, because Amendment 3's operative words are the paper's own stated purpose FOR INCLUDING the component, and this paper states that purpose twice and both times it is fairness: "a dynamic reward-penalty strategy to enforce fair, adaptive participation over training rounds" (Sec. 1) and "(iii) encourage participant engagement" (Sec. 4). The competing evidence is a results-section attribution, quoted as this row's C-e, which says the resilience comes from "differential privacy noise, fair participant selection, and secure aggregation" jointly filtering malicious updates. That sentence is an account of an observed effect, not a purpose for inclusion, and its phrase "fair participant selection" is in any case ambiguous between the credit ledger and the k-nearest selection that the paper elsewhere describes as selecting "the most reliable ones". Rule 3 points the same way. A5 should state the application rule this row establishes: PURPOSE FOR INCLUSION BEATS ATTRIBUTED EFFECT, and where a paper gives both, the row quotes both.

AMENDMENT 3 LOWERS A CODE HERE, WHICH RESTORES THE BALANCE THE EARLIER ROWS HAD UPSET. Fedward, LASA, RKD and Fed-DPRoC are four rows where the amendment RAISED a code by finding a defense purpose behind an innocuous-sounding operation; the disclosure that it could only lower rates was wrong in that direction. DSFL is the clean case in the intended direction: three of the four things a name-based reading would count are excluded on the paper's own words, and the count falls below two. Both directions are now attested and A5 reports both.

IT IS ALSO THE FRAME'S SHARPEST INSTANCE OF THE PRIVACY CLASS'S THIRD CONFIGURATION. The privacy substrate is not decorative and not separable: the dual-server additive secret sharing is what makes the distances computable without either server seeing an update, so the defense runs INSIDE the privacy mechanism, as in FORTA's DFT. But unlike FORTA, the privacy machinery here is also the paper's headline contribution and its main novelty claim against LSFL. The frame now has four configurations of the privacy class: privacy excluded and the paper still composes two defenses (DDFed); privacy load-bearing for the defense's arithmetic (FORTA, DSFL); privacy as one of two paired PROPERTIES rather than mechanisms (DP-BREM, DSFL); and privacy as an excluded headline contribution whose exclusion relocates C-a onto an incidental component (Fed-DPRoC).
